title: Benchmark Methodology: Runtime, KV Cache & VPC Deep Dive
summary: Deep dive on benchmark methodology for apples-to-apples comparisons across hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem) deployments. Covered prompt set design, load generation, KV cache behavior, batching effects, quantization tradeoffs, network E2E latency in VPC, and proposed benchmark plan + artifacts to share.
action_items: Avery Kim: Share benchmark worksheet and reproducible load scripts (due 2026-02-24)
Jordan Patel: Spin up Dedicated test cluster with quantized model variants and share access (due 2026-02-27)
Priya Singh (Nimbus): Provide representative prompt set and SAML test account for VPC access (due 2026-02-25)
Liam O'Connor: Run initial internal load-run and record tail-latency snapshots, share logs (due 2026-03-02)
next_steps: Redwood to share reproducible load generator (k6 + custom RT feeder) and prompt set template
Schedule 2-hour hands-on bench run with Nimbus engineers (propose 2026-03-04)
Exchange security checklist / VPC onboarding docs and sign NDA addendum if needed
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-02-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood Product); Sofia, Liam, Priya, Oliver (Nimbus)

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll get started. I see all the Nimbus folks on the line, thanks for making time. This is a benchmark methodology deep dive - want to make sure our apples-to-apples comparisons cover runtime, KV cache, batching, quant, and VPC network impacts.

[02:10] Sofia: Great, yeah we've been trying to compare hosted vs our VPC private deployment. Our internal numbers look noisy, especially around tail latency when cache miss rates spike.

[04:05] Jordan: Totally. To start, can you confirm your main success criteria? Is it p50/p95 latency, and cost per 1M tokens, or throughput?

[04:30] Sofia: Primary is p95 under our SLO of 250ms for short-chat flows. Secondary is cost and then mem footprint for on-prem GPU constraints.

[06:00] Oliver: Also conversation state - we use long context >2k tokens sometimes, so KV cache behavior is critical. We've seen weird regen behavior when the KV hits get invalidated.

[07:20] Jordan: Right, so we should instrument KV cache hit/miss rate, eviction patterns, and make sure the load generator reproduces your session stickiness. For apples-to-apples, same prompt set, same temperature, same seq lengths, and same request pacing.

[09:45] Liam: Quick question on batching. In our hosted runs we saw averaging that looked better, but when we forced low-latency single-request mode it blew up. How do you recommend we compare batch-optimized throughput vs low-latency single-shot?

[11:15] Maya: Good point - in our benchmarks we recommend two modes: latency mode (batch size 1, emphasis on per-request tail) and throughput mode (sustained qps with larger batching). For throughput, measure tokens/sec and cost/unit; for latency mode, measure p50/p95/p99, but make sure batching algorithms and max-wait timers are identical across deployments.

[13:40] Sofia: Regarding quantization - is quantized model behavior deterministic? We worry about quality regressions if we switch to int8 or 4-bit for cost reasons.

[14:10] Jordan: It's not perfectly deterministic across implementations, and quality can vary with quant scheme. Our recommendation: include a prompt set with golden outputs or an eval suite (RHF-ish evals) and compare logits/EM/ROUGE or embedding cosine similarity. Also keep a holdout of prompts that are sensitive to quant.

[16:05] Priya: For VPC/on-prem, network adds E2E latency. How do you isolate model inference latency vs network?

[16:40] Jordan: Instrumentation: record client-side request start, front-door router time, model-serving start/finish, and response arrival. In VPC we can run a micro-benchmark where the client sits in the same VPC to measure baseline intra-node latency, then add controlled network delay to emulate remote zones. We'll provide a tracing hook or a lightweight p99 snapshot exporter.

[18:55] Oliver: We noticed KV cache behavior differs between multi-tenant hosted and dedicated pools; evictions happen faster on shared infrastructure. Any guidance?

[19:30] Avery: Yes, isolation matters. Dedicated will provision larger KV cache capacity per shard and reduce eviction churn. For fair tests, vendor-provide same working set size and pin model/configs. We'll run a dedicated cluster with the same sequence distribution to show the improvement.

[22:00] Sofia: About load generation - what's the recommended toolchain? We've used locust and JMeter, but they don't mimic sticky sessions well.

[22:30] Jordan: We built a reproducible suite: k6 for qps shaping + a small RT feeder to replay session traces including user think time and prompt prefixes. We'll share the repo. Key is to record realistic session traces from production and parameterize rate, concurrency, and skew. Include a synthetic spike run to exercise cache miss storms.

[25:15] Liam: How do we ensure the model variants are comparable? Like, different quant levels, fused kernels, or differing kernel libraries across hardware.

[26:00] Jordan: Document everything: model family, weights, tokenizer version, quant scheme, kernel lib (e.g., cuBLAS vs Cutlass vs Triton kernels), compiler flags, GPU type, driver and CUDA versions. For apples-to-apples, if you can't run the same kernel, at least match precision and report all infra diffs. We'll provide a canonical bench matrix.

[28:40] Oliver: Is it okay to compare across different GPUs? We have A100s in cloud but 80GB rtx on-prem.

[29:05] Maya: You can compare, but normalize results by hardware performance (e.g., TFLOPS/core, memory bandwidth) and report per-token energy/cost too. Better is to compare SLO attainment (p95 and throughput) at the operating point you care about.

[31:20] Sofia: On the prompt set - we want to stress long-context retrieval and short-turn conversational. How many prompts per category do you recommend?

[31:45] Jordan: We suggest 500-1k examples per workload type: short (<=64 tokens), medium (256-1024), and long (>1024). Include randomized prefixes and keystream repeats to test cache warm/cold behavior. Keep a 20% holdout for quality/regression checks.

[34:10] Priya: Can Redwood's runtime export per-request KV hit metadata? We need to validate cache efficiency.

[34:35] Jordan: Yes, runtime emits KV hits/misses per request and per-shard metrics. We'll enable a debug mode that tags requests with a small summary (hit=true/false, cache_size, eviction_count). We'll sanitize logs before sharing.

[36:50] Liam: Regarding quantization, what quant profiles do you support? Any recommended starting profiles?

[37:10] Jordan: We have q8_0, q4_0, q4_1 families and a mixed-precision pathway. Start with q8 if you want minimal quality impact; q4_1 often gives best cost/quality for many LLMs but do the eval suite. We'll include recommended baseline profiles in the worksheet.

[39:40] Sofia: Network egress costs are a concern for us if we go hosted. For VPC/on-prem, there's overhead in ops complexity. Can you summarize tradeoffs?

[40:05] Avery: Hosted: easiest onboarding, predictable API, but egress/cross-region costs. Dedicated: reserved capacity with isolation and lower per-token variance. VPC/On-prem: full data control but upfront ops and network tuning. The benchmark must measure not just latency but operational overhead and failure modes - e.g., node loss, autoscaling cold-starts, and cache rebuild time.

[42:20] Oliver: For autoscaling, should we warm the KV cache? Otherwise first wave will all be cache misses.

[42:45] Jordan: Warm-up is critical. Use a replay of representative sessions at low rate to pre-populate the KV cache, then ramp traffic. We'll include warm-up scripts that reproduce conversational continuity and key frequency distribution.

[45:00] Priya: Can you help us with secrets and SSO for the VPC tests? We have SAML SSO and KMS policy requirements.

[45:30] Avery: Yes, we'll hand over the security checklist and a minimal SAML integration plan. For KMS, we'll test with a sample wrapped key; for on-prem, we can mimic HSM behavior. We'll also propose an NDA addendum for bench artifacts.

[48:15] Sofia: Let's capture expected deliverables after this call.

[48:40] Jordan: Deliverables: reproducible load generator repo, benchmark worksheet (with columns for infra, model, quant, prompt set, trace id), Dedicated test cluster access (read-only for metrics), and a proposed 2-hour bench run date.

[50:10] Liam: On the bench run day, can Redwood run the workload while Nimbus watches logs? We want to see end-to-end traces.

[50:30] Maya: Yes, we recommend a shared live-run: Redwood runs the load against either Dedicated or a VPC staging customer instance, shares Grafana and traces, and captures p50/p95/p99 and KV hit rates. We'll record the run and provide artifacts.

[52:00] Oliver: A couple of nitty-gritty items - how do you measure cost-per-token consistently? Do you include infra amortization?

[52:25] Avery: We provide a unit-economics worksheet: raw infra cost (cloud/GPU hours), software license, and ops time estimate. For on-prem, customers should plug in their capex amortization; we'll show cost-per-1M-tokens under different utilization assumptions.

[54:10] Priya: Any gotchas on metric alignment? We use prom counters and tracing but sometimes clocks drift between nodes.

[54:35] Jordan: Use synchronized NTP and prefer relative latencies. For absolute timing, run a short sync job and annotate traces. Also, sample tracing at p99 rate to avoid overhead.

[56:00] Sofia: Okay this is helpful. Let's recap next steps.

[56:20] Avery: Recap - Redwood to share: load generator repo + prompt templates, benchmark worksheet, quant baseline profiles, and security/VPC onboarding docs. Nimbus to share: prompt set sample, SAML test account, and internal session traces for replay. Schedule bench run (proposed 2026-03-04).

[58:10] Liam: We'll aim to provide the session traces and SAML creds by 2026-02-25.

[59:55] Jordan: One more note - when you run the bench, capture both cold-start and warm cache scenarios and tag them in the result spreadsheet. Cold-starts can skew averages if not labeled.

[61:30] Oliver: Also we found a previously unnoticed issue where certain tokenizer edge-cases produce very long kv keys leading to higher memory use - worth checking.

[62:00] Jordan: We'll add a tokenizer edge-case test to the prompt set and track kv key length distribution.

[64:15] Sofia: Thanks everyone. We'll expect the materials.

[65:00] Avery: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the links and a calendar invite for the bench run.

[75:00] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript has occasional mis-transcriptions, some names spelled differently in live notes. Attachments referenced: shared spreadsheet link (redwood.com/bench-worksheet), load repo (github.com/redwood/bench-repro), security checklist (redwood.com/security/vpc-onprem-checklist) - these will be shared in follow-up.
